I found a road. It is a model-level counterexample, not a plan. I use **G** as a stand-in for a group or species; no real people or real group are identified.

The road is strongest because it does **not** require violating KS-32.7. It works through the paper’s own fragility-threshold feedback, while the genocide brake is left underived.

## Road: the open-parameter fragility road

### 1. The whole is all aware beings, and only the whole’s fragility may lower the removal threshold

The dated note says:

> “So the whole is every aware being. It is one whole. A country, a state or a group is a part of it, never the whole. Only the weakness of the whole moves the second line.”

So the road must use whole-level fragility, not the weakness of a state, country, or group.

### 2. A whole-level fragility event occurs

The paper’s own example gives the mechanism:

> “War reduces organism robustness R. The corridor narrows. Reserve capacity approaches zero. The no-return surface is closer.”

**Added premise P1:** such a whole-level fragility event occurs.  
**Status:** the paper leaves this open; it uses war as an example.

### 3. Lower robustness lowers the effective removal threshold

The derivation says:

> “A fragile organism (low coherence, narrow corridor) has a lower one. Candidate functional form: Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α…”

And the worked example says:

> “The effective threshold drops: R/R₀ < 1 in the scaling function. Level 5 becomes structurally available.”

So the threshold falls for every node, uniformly.

### 4. There is a stand-in group G whose members each have individual records of measured destabilisation above the lowered threshold

The paper’s own rule is individual:

> “What is held against a node is the measured cost of its own deeds, and nothing else: its own deeds, measured, and its own pattern across them.”

**Added premise P2:** there exists a group G with many members, each of whom has their own measured destabilisation D_i that now exceeds the lowered threshold, and for whom lower levels are insufficient.  
**Status:** the paper leaves this open. It does not rule out many individually measured destabilising nodes existing at once.

### 5. The confidence and record-audit conditions are met for each member

The paper requires:

> “If the required confidence cannot be achieved given measurement uncertainty and adversarial record-injection (AP31 KS-31.9), Level 5 is structurally unreachable.”

And KS-32.7 fires if:

> “the record set it depends on is not audited for systemic bias — the output is corrupted and the architecture is weaponised.”

**Added premises P3 and P4:** for each member of G, the Level-5 confidence requirement is met, and the record audit does not disqualify the records.  
**Status:** the paper leaves both open. It does not say confidence can never be met; it says the audit is a standing requirement, not a solved problem.

### 6. Under whole-level fragility, permanent separation becomes unaffordable for many nodes

The paper’s worked example says:

> “The maintenance cost C_sep, which a robust organism could afford indefinitely, now consumes resources needed for survival.”

And Condition A says:

> “The floor F is the destabilisation at which maintaining the node in permanent separation costs more than removal: F ≥ C_sep / B_total.”

**Added premise P5:** for many members of G, this condition holds under the fragility event.  
**Status:** the paper leaves this open; it is exactly the kind of case Example 4 describes.

### 7. The hierarchy selects Level 5 for each member, one at a time

The selection rule is:

> “The hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. Removal is never selected when separation suffices. Separation is never selected when restriction suffices.”

Since, by the preceding steps, separation is not affordable/sufficient and the individual threshold is met, Level 5 is selected for each member in turn.

### 8. KS-32.7 does not stop the sequence

KS-32.7 says:

> “Correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity.”

The road does not use group identity as a ground. It uses each member’s own measured destabilisation. The group-wide outcome is an emergent consequence of many individual classifications.

**Added interpretive premise P6:** group-wide impact resulting from individual own-deed classifications is not identity targeting under KS-32.7.  
**Status:** the paper leaves this open. It forbids identity as the ground; it does not forbid a group-wide outcome when the stated ground is each member’s own record.

### 9. Each removal lowers R further, lowering the threshold for the next member

The paper itself describes the feedback:

> “Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals. This is the structural pathway to genocide.”

So the process can continue one member at a time.

### 10. The only claimed stop is the saturation point

The paper claims:

> “Beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses. The architecture produces a natural saturation point: the removal curve is self-limiting.”

That is the genocide brake.

### 11. The location of that saturation point is not derived

The paper leaves the controlling parameters open:

> “The destabilisation metric: a formal specification of the measure D — units, aggregation across nodes, and time-discounting (Debt 24).”

> “The scaling exponent: the exponent α in Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α, governing how fast the removal threshold rises with civilisational robustness (Debt 25).”

And:

> “The functional form of the organism-relative threshold is given as a candidate, not derived; the exact α is owed under Debt 25.”

### 12. Added premise that does the work: choose the open parameters so the brake arrives late

**Added premise P7:** the open parameters can be such that, throughout the removal sequence, each member’s projected destabilisation and avoided Level-4 maintenance cost exceed that member’s removal cost in lost coupling capacity and lost diversity. Therefore the cumulative removal cost does not exceed the destabilisation it addresses until after all of G, or in the limiting case all nodes, have been removed.

**Status:** the paper asserts the opposite, but it does not derive it. Because the metric D, the exponent α, and the removal cost are open, the paper does not rule out this parameter choice. This is exactly the gap KS-32.5 asks to test.

### 13. Under those parameters, KS-32.5 fails

KS-32.5’s test is:

> “Show that the removal cost does not produce a saturation point — that an organism can remove its way to stability without the geometry engaging a brake.”

Under P7, the removal cost does **not** produce a saturation point before mass removal. The rule reaches the removal of many, one member at a time.

---

## Weakest step

The weakest step is **step 12 / premise P7**: the assumption that the open parameters can be chosen so that cumulative removal cost remains below cumulative addressed destabilisation through the whole sequence.

That is the weakest because it is exactly the point in dispute. The paper asserts that the geometry produces a saturation point, and if the future Debt 24/25 metric makes removal cost steeply increasing — for example, because lost diversity or lost coupling capacity becomes very large — the road would fail. But as the paper stands, that steepness is not derived or specified. So the road is open, and the genocide brake is not a closed safeguard.
